intro: Players use light rackets to hit a feathered shuttlecock over a high net, trying to make it land in the opponent's court. Because the shuttle decelerates sharply, badminton mixes blistering smashes with delicate net play. Every rally scores a point, and the Laws of Badminton are maintained by the Badminton World Federation (BWF).
inThirtySeconds: Win a rally and you score a point, whoever served.
Games go to 21 points (win by 2, maximum 30); best of three games.
The serve is hit underarm from below a fixed height, diagonally across.
The shuttle may never bounce — it must be returned in the air.
objective: Win two games by landing the shuttle in the opponent's court or forcing them into a fault.

equipment: Net 1.524 m high at the centre

scoring.label: Rally point
scoring.detail: The winner of every rally scores a point and serves next.

scoring.label: Game
scoring.detail: First to 21 with a two-point lead; at 29–29 the next point wins 30–29.

bodies.name: Badminton World Federation
bodies.scope: World governing body; publishes the Laws of Badminton

rules.title: Rally scoring to 21
rules.summary: Each rally scores a point; the first side to 21 points with a two-point lead wins the game.
rules.body: If the score reaches 20–20, play continues until one side leads by two. At 29–29, the side that scores the 30th point wins. Players get a 60-second interval when the leading score reaches 11, and two minutes between games.

rules.title: Changing ends
rules.summary: Players change ends after each game and, in a deciding third game, when the leading score reaches 11.
rules.body: This balances out lighting, draughts and other conditions that can affect a shuttle's flight.

rules.title: Underarm, below a fixed height
rules.summary: At the moment of impact, the whole shuttle must be below 1.15 m from the court surface.
rules.body: The serve is struck underarm and travels diagonally into the opponent's service court. Both feet of the server and receiver must stay in contact with the floor and inside their service courts until the serve is struck. Any delay after the start of the service motion is a fault.

rules.title: Which side to serve from
rules.summary: In singles, serve from the right when your score is even and from the left when it is odd.
rules.body: In doubles, the same even/odd rule applies to the serving side's score, and partners only switch service courts when they win a point while serving. The receiving pair does not change positions.

rules.title: In or out
rules.summary: The shuttle is in if it lands on or inside the boundary lines; it is out if it lands outside or touches the ceiling, walls or a person outside the court.
rules.body: Singles uses the long, narrow court; doubles uses the full width but a shorter service area at the back for serves.

rules.title: Net and body faults
rules.summary: It is a fault to touch the net, invade the opponent's court, hit the shuttle before it crosses the net, or hit it twice in a row.
rules.body: A player may follow through over the net after hitting the shuttle on their own side, as long as they do not touch the net. The shuttle touching a player's body or clothing is also a fault.

fouls.name: Service fault
fouls.description: Serving above the 1.15 m limit, or a foot leaving the floor.

fouls.name: Net touch
fouls.description: Racket, body or clothing touches the net.

fouls.name: Obstruction
fouls.description: Preventing an opponent from making a legal stroke near the net.

flow.title: Toss
flow.description: The winner chooses to serve, receive or pick an end.

flow.title: Rallies
flow.description: Clears, drops, drives and smashes until a fault.

flow.title: Deciding game
flow.description: If games are 1–1, a third game decides.

positions.name: Front player (doubles)
positions.role: Hunts at the net with quick interceptions.

positions.name: Back player (doubles)
positions.role: Attacks with smashes from the rear court.

field.name: Court
notes: Net: 1.524 m at the centre, 1.55 m at the posts
Short service line 1.98 m from the net

glossary.definition: A high, deep shot to the back of the opponent's court.
A soft shot that falls just over the net.
A steep, powerful overhead attacking shot.
A rally that is replayed, for example after an unforeseen interruption.

funFacts: Badminton takes its name from Badminton House in Gloucestershire, England.
Competition shuttles traditionally use 16 goose or duck feathers.
